docs.title: kalman_gain(particles: Float[Array, 'N_e N_x'], obs_particles: Float[Array, 'N_e N_y'], obs_noise: lx.AbstractLinearOperator, *, solver: gaussx.AbstractSolverStrategy | None = None, dense_innovation: bool | None = None) -> Float[Array, 'N_x N_y']
docs.text:
Kalman gain from an ensemble and its image in observation space.

G = Σ̂_xy Σ̂_y⁻¹,   Σ̂_y = Σ̂_h + Σ_ε

Wraps gaussx.ensemble_kalman_gain and fixes bessel=True, the divisor N_ℰ − 1. Σ̂_y is assembled by one of two routes, which agree to round-off. With U = H̃ᵀ / √(N_ℰ − 1), the Woodbury route solves through

Σ̂_y⁻¹ = Σ_ε⁻¹ − Σ_ε⁻¹ U (I + Uᵀ Σ_ε⁻¹ U)⁻¹ Uᵀ Σ_ε⁻¹
  • Woodbury, the default when N_ℰ < D_y: Σ̂_y is a gaussx.LowRankUpdate of Σ_ε, solved by structural dispatch at O(N_ℰ² D_y + N_ℰ³), and a structured Σ_ε is never materialised.
  • Dense, the default when N_ℰ ≥ D_y: Σ̂_y is formed as a (D_y, D_y) matrix and solved directly at O(N_ℰ D_y² + D_y³), because the capacitance would be the larger matrix. It also handles a positive semi-definite Σ_ε, which Woodbury cannot.
Algorithm
  1. Choose the route for Σ̂_y from the shapes or dense_innovation.
  2. Form the cross-covariance Σ̂_xy.
  3. Assemble Σ̂_y densely, or as a low-rank update of Σ_ε.
  4. Solve for the gain G = Σ̂_xy Σ̂_y⁻¹ row by row.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default particles Float[Array, 'N_e N_x']

Prior ensemble x⁽ᵉ⁾ in state space, one row per member.

required obs_particles Float[Array, 'N_e N_y']

Its image h⁽ᵉ⁾ = h(x⁽ᵉ⁾) in observation space. A nonlinear h is linearised implicitly by the ensemble.

required obs_noise AbstractLinearOperator

Observation-error covariance Σ_ε.

required solver AbstractSolverStrategy | None

Solver strategy for Σ̂_y; None uses structural dispatch. A matrix-free strategy wants dense_innovation=False, so that it gets the structured operator.

None dense_innovation bool | None

Whether to form the (D_y, D_y) Σ̂_y densely. None chooses by shape; True and False force the dense and the Woodbury route.

None

Returns:

Type Description Float[Array, 'N_x N_y']

The dense Kalman gain G. It is consumed once by the analysis and is usually

Float[Array, 'N_x N_y']

small, since D_y counts the observations.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the ensembles have different sizes, obs_noise is not (D_y, D_y), or N_ℰ < 2.

Examples:

Three members, with the first component observed:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import filterax
>>> particles = jnp.array([[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0], [2.0, 0.0]])
>>> obs_particles = particles[:, :1]
>>> obs_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.5 * jnp.ones(1))
>>> gain = filterax.kalman_gain(particles, obs_particles, obs_noise)
>>> gain.shape
(2, 1)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(gain, jnp.array([[2.0 / 3.0], [0.0]])))
True

The two routes agree to round-off:

>>> woodbury = filterax.kalman_gain(
...     particles, obs_particles, obs_noise, dense_innovation=False
... )
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(gain, woodbury, atol=1e-4))
True

One member has no sample covariance:

>>> filterax.kalman_gain(
...     particles[:1], obs_particles[:1], obs_noise
... )
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: Bessel correction requires J >= 2 particles (divisor is J - 1);
got J=1. Pass bessel=False for a maximum-likelihood divisor.
Source code in src/filterax/_primitives/_gain.py 
def kalman_gain(
    particles: Float[Array, "N_e N_x"],
    obs_particles: Float[Array, "N_e N_y"],
    obs_noise: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    *,
    solver: gaussx.AbstractSolverStrategy | None = None,
    dense_innovation: bool | None = None,
) -> Float[Array, "N_x N_y"]:
    """Kalman gain from an ensemble and its image in observation space.

        G = Σ̂_xy Σ̂_y⁻¹,   Σ̂_y = Σ̂_h + Σ_ε

    Wraps `gaussx.ensemble_kalman_gain` and fixes ``bessel=True``, the divisor
    N_ℰ − 1. Σ̂_y is assembled by one of two routes, which agree to round-off. With
    U = H̃ᵀ / √(N_ℰ − 1), the Woodbury route solves through

        Σ̂_y⁻¹ = Σ_ε⁻¹ − Σ_ε⁻¹ U (I + Uᵀ Σ_ε⁻¹ U)⁻¹ Uᵀ Σ_ε⁻¹

    - **Woodbury**, the default when N_ℰ < D_y: Σ̂_y is a `gaussx.LowRankUpdate` of
      Σ_ε, solved by structural dispatch at O(N_ℰ² D_y + N_ℰ³), and a structured Σ_ε
      is never materialised.
    - **Dense**, the default when N_ℰ ≥ D_y: Σ̂_y is formed as a (D_y, D_y) matrix and
      solved directly at O(N_ℰ D_y² + D_y³), because the capacitance would be the
      larger matrix. It also handles a positive semi-definite Σ_ε, which Woodbury
      cannot.

    Algorithm:
        1. Choose the route for Σ̂_y from the shapes or ``dense_innovation``.
        2. Form the cross-covariance Σ̂_xy.
        3. Assemble Σ̂_y densely, or as a low-rank update of Σ_ε.
        4. Solve for the gain G = Σ̂_xy Σ̂_y⁻¹ row by row.

    Args:
        particles: Prior ensemble x⁽ᵉ⁾ in state space, one row per member.
        obs_particles: Its image h⁽ᵉ⁾ = h(x⁽ᵉ⁾) in observation space. A nonlinear h
            is linearised implicitly by the ensemble.
        obs_noise: Observation-error covariance Σ_ε.
        solver: Solver strategy for Σ̂_y; ``None`` uses structural dispatch. A
            matrix-free strategy wants ``dense_innovation=False``, so that it gets
            the structured operator.
        dense_innovation: Whether to form the (D_y, D_y) Σ̂_y densely. ``None``
            chooses by shape; ``True`` and ``False`` force the dense and the
            Woodbury route.

    Returns:
        The dense Kalman gain G. It is consumed once by the analysis and is usually
        small, since D_y counts the observations.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the ensembles have different sizes, ``obs_noise`` is not
            (D_y, D_y), or N_ℰ < 2.

    Examples:
        Three members, with the first component observed:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import filterax
        >>> particles = jnp.array([[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0], [2.0, 0.0]])
        >>> obs_particles = particles[:, :1]
        >>> obs_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.5 * jnp.ones(1))
        >>> gain = filterax.kalman_gain(particles, obs_particles, obs_noise)
        >>> gain.shape
        (2, 1)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(gain, jnp.array([[2.0 / 3.0], [0.0]])))
        True

        The two routes agree to round-off:

        >>> woodbury = filterax.kalman_gain(
        ...     particles, obs_particles, obs_noise, dense_innovation=False
        ... )
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(gain, woodbury, atol=1e-4))
        True

        One member has no sample covariance:

        >>> filterax.kalman_gain(
        ...     particles[:1], obs_particles[:1], obs_noise
        ... )  # doctest: +NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        ValueError: Bessel correction requires J >= 2 particles (divisor is J - 1);
        got J=1. Pass bessel=False for a maximum-likelihood divisor.
    """
    # G = Σ̂_xy Σ̂_y⁻¹
    return gaussx.ensemble_kalman_gain(
        particles,
        obs_particles,
        obs_noise,
        solver=solver,
        bessel=True,
        dense_innovation=dense_innovation,
    )

docs.title: log_likelihood(innovation: Float[Array, ' N_y'], innovation_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator, *, solver: gaussx.AbstractSolverStrategy | None = None) -> Float[Array, '']
docs.text:
Gaussian log-probability of a mean residual.

log 𝒩(r̄; 0, Σ_y) = −½ (D_y log 2π + log det Σ_y + r̄ᵀ Σ_y⁻¹ r̄)

Wraps gaussx.gaussian_log_prob, so both terms go through gaussx's dispatch: when Σ_y is a gaussx.LowRankUpdate, the standard case, the log-determinant uses the matrix-determinant lemma and the solve uses Woodbury, each at O(N_ℰ² D_y + N_ℰ³).

This is the training signal of differentiable data assimilation: its gradient with respect to dynamics or observation-model parameters gives an end-to-end learning loop without ever forming Σ_y.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default innovation Float[Array, ' N_y']

Mean residual r̄ = y − h̄.

required innovation_cov AbstractLinearOperator

Innovation covariance Σ_y, typically from innovation_covariance.

required solver AbstractSolverStrategy | None

Solver strategy for Σ_y; None uses structural dispatch.

None

Returns:

Type Description Float[Array, '']

The scalar log-probability.

Examples:

A unit covariance leaves −½ (2 log 2π + ‖r̄‖²):

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import filterax
>>> innovation = jnp.array([0.5, -0.5])
>>> innovation_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(2))
>>> value = filterax.log_likelihood(innovation, innovation_cov)
>>> round(float(value), 4)
-2.0879

A dense and a structured Σ_y agree:

>>> dense = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(filterax.log_likelihood(innovation, dense), value))
True
Source code in src/filterax/_primitives/_likelihood.py 
def log_likelihood(
    innovation: Float[Array, " N_y"],
    innovation_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    *,
    solver: gaussx.AbstractSolverStrategy | None = None,
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """Gaussian log-probability of a mean residual.

        log 𝒩(r̄; 0, Σ_y) = −½ (D_y log 2π + log det Σ_y + r̄ᵀ Σ_y⁻¹ r̄)

    Wraps `gaussx.gaussian_log_prob`, so both terms go through gaussx's dispatch: when
    Σ_y is a `gaussx.LowRankUpdate`, the standard case, the log-determinant uses the
    matrix-determinant lemma and the solve uses Woodbury, each at
    O(N_ℰ² D_y + N_ℰ³).

    This is the training signal of differentiable data assimilation: its gradient with
    respect to dynamics or observation-model parameters gives an end-to-end learning
    loop without ever forming Σ_y.

    Args:
        innovation: Mean residual r̄ = y − h̄.
        innovation_cov: Innovation covariance Σ_y, typically from
            `innovation_covariance`.
        solver: Solver strategy for Σ_y; ``None`` uses structural dispatch.

    Returns:
        The scalar log-probability.

    Examples:
        A unit covariance leaves −½ (2 log 2π + ‖r̄‖²):

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import filterax
        >>> innovation = jnp.array([0.5, -0.5])
        >>> innovation_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(2))
        >>> value = filterax.log_likelihood(innovation, innovation_cov)
        >>> round(float(value), 4)
        -2.0879

        A dense and a structured Σ_y agree:

        >>> dense = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(2), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(filterax.log_likelihood(innovation, dense), value))
        True
    """
    zero_mean = jnp.zeros_like(innovation)
    # log 𝒩(r̄; 0, Σ_y)
    return gaussx.gaussian_log_prob(
        zero_mean, innovation_cov, innovation, solver=solver
    )

def innovation_covariance(
    obs_particles: Float[Array, "N_e N_y"],
    obs_noise: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
) -> gaussx.LowRankUpdate:
    """Innovation covariance of an ensemble as a low-rank update of Σ_ε.

        Σ̂_y = Σ̂_h + Σ_ε = Σ_ε + U Uᵀ,   U = H̃ᵀ / √(N_ℰ − 1)

    Takes the factor U from `gaussx.ensemble_covariance` with ``bessel=True`` and
    composes it with Σ_ε, keeping Σ_ε's structure. Downstream linear algebra exploits
    the term of rank at most N_ℰ − 1 without densifying.

    Args:
        obs_particles: Forecast ensemble h⁽ᵉ⁾ in observation space, one row per member.
        obs_noise: Observation-error covariance Σ_ε.

    Returns:
        A `gaussx.LowRankUpdate` holding Σ̂_y.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If N_ℰ < 2, or ``obs_noise`` is not (D_y, D_y).

    Examples:
        Two members with Σ̂_h = 0.5 and Σ_ε = 0.1:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import filterax
        >>> obs_particles = jnp.array([[0.0], [1.0]])
        >>> obs_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.1 * jnp.ones(1))
        >>> covariance = filterax.innovation_covariance(obs_particles, obs_noise)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(covariance.as_matrix(), jnp.array([[0.6]])))
        True

        It solves without being materialised:

        >>> import gaussx
        >>> gaussx.solve(covariance, jnp.ones(1)).shape
        (1,)
    """
    # Σ̂_h = U Uᵀ,   U = H̃ᵀ / √(N_ℰ − 1)
    obs_ensemble_covariance = gaussx.ensemble_covariance(obs_particles, bessel=True)
    # Σ̂_y = Σ_ε + U Uᵀ
    return gaussx.LowRankUpdate(obs_noise, obs_ensemble_covariance.U)

Innovation diagnostics of a forecast ensemble.

r̄ = y − h̄,   Σ̂_y = Σ̂_h + Σ_ε,   Σ̂_y^−½ r̄,   log 𝒩(r̄; 0, Σ̂_y)

The whitened residual serves χ² and Desroziers-style consistency checks: under a correctly specified Σ̂_y each component is a unit-variance Gaussian. It uses the principal root through gaussx.sqrt_inv_matmul, a contour quadrature of shifted solves, so it does not depend on the order of the observations. With 30 nodes, its squared norm matches r̄ᵀ Σ̂_y⁻¹ r̄ to about 1e-10 (relative, float64) up to a condition number of 1e6.

With N_ℰ ≤ D_y, the whitener goes through Woodbury and Σ̂_y is never materialised. Otherwise each Woodbury solve would factor the larger (N_ℰ, N_ℰ) capacitance, so Σ̂_y is formed densely. The log-likelihood comes from ensemble_log_likelihood.

Algorithm
  1. Map the members through h, and form r̄ and Σ̂_y.
  2. Choose the operator for the whitener from the shapes.
  3. Evaluate the log-likelihood.
  4. Whiten r̄ with 30 quadrature nodes.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default particles Float[Array, 'N_e N_x']

Forecast ensemble x⁽ᵉ⁾, one row per member.

required obs Float[Array, ' N_y']

Observation vector y.

required obs_op Callable[[Float[Array, ' N_x']], Float[Array, ' N_y']]

Observation operator h on one state, mapped over the ensemble here.

required obs_noise AbstractLinearOperator

Observation-error covariance Σ_ε.

required solver AbstractSolverStrategy | None

Solver strategy for the log-likelihood's log-determinant and solve. The whitened residual always uses structural dispatch.

None

Returns:

Type Description InnovationStatistics

An InnovationStatistics mapping with innovation, innovation_cov,

InnovationStatistics

normalized_innovation and log_likelihood.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If N_ℰ < 2.

Examples:

Two members, with the first component observed:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import filterax
>>> particles = jnp.array([[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
>>> obs = jnp.array([0.5])
>>> obs_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(1))
>>> stats = filterax.innovation_statistics(
...     particles, obs, lambda state: state[:1], obs_noise
... )
>>> stats["innovation"].tolist()
[0.0]
>>> round(float(stats["log_likelihood"]), 4)
-1.1217

One member cannot supply a sample covariance:

>>> filterax.innovation_statistics(
...     particles[:1], obs, lambda state: state[:1], obs_noise
... )

...

Bessel-corrected estimators to be well-defined; got N_e=1.

def innovation_statistics(
    particles: Float[Array, "N_e N_x"],
    obs: Float[Array, " N_y"],
    obs_op: Callable[[Float[Array, " N_x"]], Float[Array, " N_y"]],
    obs_noise: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    *,
    solver: gaussx.AbstractSolverStrategy | None = None,
) -> InnovationStatistics:
    """Innovation diagnostics of a forecast ensemble.

        r̄ = y − h̄,   Σ̂_y = Σ̂_h + Σ_ε,   Σ̂_y^−½ r̄,   log 𝒩(r̄; 0, Σ̂_y)

    The whitened residual serves χ² and Desroziers-style consistency checks: under a
    correctly specified Σ̂_y each component is a unit-variance Gaussian. It uses the
    principal root through `gaussx.sqrt_inv_matmul`, a contour quadrature of shifted
    solves, so it does not depend on the order of the observations. With 30 nodes, its
    squared norm matches r̄ᵀ Σ̂_y⁻¹ r̄ to about 1e-10 (relative, float64) up to a
    condition number of 1e6.

    With N_ℰ ≤ D_y, the whitener goes through Woodbury and Σ̂_y is never materialised.
    Otherwise each Woodbury solve would factor the larger (N_ℰ, N_ℰ) capacitance, so
    Σ̂_y is formed densely. The log-likelihood comes from `ensemble_log_likelihood`.

    Algorithm:
        1. Map the members through h, and form r̄ and Σ̂_y.
        2. Choose the operator for the whitener from the shapes.
        3. Evaluate the log-likelihood.
        4. Whiten r̄ with 30 quadrature nodes.

    Args:
        particles: Forecast ensemble x⁽ᵉ⁾, one row per member.
        obs: Observation vector y.
        obs_op: Observation operator h on one state, mapped over the ensemble here.
        obs_noise: Observation-error covariance Σ_ε.
        solver: Solver strategy for the log-likelihood's log-determinant and solve.
            The whitened residual always uses structural dispatch.

    Returns:
        An `InnovationStatistics` mapping with ``innovation``, ``innovation_cov``,
        ``normalized_innovation`` and ``log_likelihood``.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If N_ℰ < 2.

    Examples:
        Two members, with the first component observed:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import filterax
        >>> particles = jnp.array([[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
        >>> obs = jnp.array([0.5])
        >>> obs_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(1))
        >>> stats = filterax.innovation_statistics(
        ...     particles, obs, lambda state: state[:1], obs_noise
        ... )
        >>> stats["innovation"].tolist()
        [0.0]
        >>> round(float(stats["log_likelihood"]), 4)
        -1.1217

        One member cannot supply a sample covariance:

        >>> filterax.innovation_statistics(
        ...     particles[:1], obs, lambda state: state[:1], obs_noise
        ... )  # doctest: +NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        ValueError: particles must contain at least 2 ensemble members for the
        Bessel-corrected estimators to be well-defined; got N_e=1.
    """
    # ensemble_mean runs first, and einx cannot size an empty ensemble.
    check_ensemble_size(particles.shape[0])
    # h⁽ᵉ⁾ = h(x⁽ᵉ⁾)
    obs_particles = jax.vmap(obs_op)(particles)
    # h̄ = (1 / N_ℰ) ∑ₑ h⁽ᵉ⁾
    obs_mean = ensemble_mean(obs_particles)
    # r̄ = y − h̄
    residual = obs - obs_mean

    # Σ̂_y = Σ_ε + U Uᵀ
    obs_covariance = innovation_covariance(obs_particles, obs_noise)
    ensemble_size, obs_size = obs_particles.shape
    # At N_ℰ = 1000, D_y = 3 the 30 Woodbury solves below take 100 s against
    # milliseconds for the (D_y, D_y) matrix.
    solve_operator = obs_covariance
    if solver is None and ensemble_size > obs_size:
        dense_covariance = obs_covariance.as_matrix()
        solve_operator = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
            dense_covariance, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
        )
    # log 𝒩(r̄; 0, Σ̂_y)
    log_prob = ensemble_log_likelihood(
        obs_particles, residual, obs_noise, solver=solver
    )

    residual_column = einx.id("obs -> obs 1", residual)
    # Σ̂_y^−½ r̄. The default 15 nodes leave a relative error of 1e-5 in its squared
    # norm at a condition number of 6.5e6.
    whitened_column = gaussx.sqrt_inv_matmul(
        solve_operator,
        residual_column,
        num_quadrature=30,
    )
    whitened = einx.id("obs 1 -> obs", whitened_column)

    return InnovationStatistics(
        innovation=residual,
        innovation_cov=obs_covariance,
        normalized_innovation=whitened,
        log_likelihood=log_prob,
    )

docs.title: perturbed_observations(key: PRNGKeyArray, obs: Float[Array, ' N_y'], obs_noise: lx.AbstractLinearOperator, n_ensemble: int) -> Float[Array, 'N_e N_y']
docs.text:
One noisy copy of the observations per ensemble member.

y⁽ᵉ⁾ = y + ε⁽ᵉ⁾,   ε⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ 𝒩(0, Σ_ε),   e ∈ ℰ

Wraps gaussx.sample_mvn, which draws ε = L z with z ~ 𝒩(0, I) and L Lᵀ = Σ_ε exactly, and chooses L by the structure of Σ_ε:

  • Diagonal: ε = √diag(Σ_ε) ⊙ z. No matrix is formed, and it costs O(N_ℰ D_y).
  • gaussx block-diagonal, Kronecker, Toeplitz and low-rank-update: a factor that keeps the structure, avoiding the cubic cost.
  • Anything else: a dense symmetric square root. It costs O(D_y³) once per call and also handles a singular Σ_ε.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key PRNGKeyArray

PRNG key consumed by this call.

required obs Float[Array, ' N_y']

Observation vector y.

required obs_noise AbstractLinearOperator

Observation-error covariance Σ_ε.

required n_ensemble int

Number of perturbed copies N_ℰ.

required

Returns:

Type Description Float[Array, 'N_e N_y']

The perturbed observations y⁽ᵉ⁾, one row per member.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If n_ensemble is below 1, or obs does not match Σ_ε.

Examples:

Four copies of two observations:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import jax.random as jr
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import filterax
>>> obs = jnp.array([1.0, 2.0])
>>> obs_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.1 * jnp.ones(2))
>>> perturbed = filterax.perturbed_observations(jr.key(0), obs, obs_noise, 4)
>>> perturbed.shape
(4, 2)

Zero noise returns the observations themselves:

>>> quiet = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.zeros(2))
>>> copies = filterax.perturbed_observations(jr.key(0), obs, quiet, 2)
>>> copies.tolist()
[[1.0, 2.0], [1.0, 2.0]]

At least one copy is needed:

>>> filterax.perturbed_observations(jr.key(0), obs, obs_noise, 0)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: num_samples must be at least 1, got 0.
References

Burgers, van Leeuwen & Evensen (1998), Mon. Wea. Rev. 126, 1719–1724.

def perturbed_observations(
    key: PRNGKeyArray,
    obs: Float[Array, " N_y"],
    obs_noise: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    n_ensemble: int,
) -> Float[Array, "N_e N_y"]:
    """One noisy copy of the observations per ensemble member.

        y⁽ᵉ⁾ = y + ε⁽ᵉ⁾,   ε⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ 𝒩(0, Σ_ε),   e ∈ ℰ

    Wraps `gaussx.sample_mvn`, which draws ε = L z with z ~ 𝒩(0, I) and L Lᵀ = Σ_ε
    exactly, and chooses L by the structure of Σ_ε:

    - Diagonal: ε = √diag(Σ_ε) ⊙ z. No matrix is formed, and it costs O(N_ℰ D_y).
    - `gaussx` block-diagonal, Kronecker, Toeplitz and low-rank-update: a factor that
      keeps the structure, avoiding the cubic cost.
    - Anything else: a dense symmetric square root. It costs O(D_y³) once per call
      and also handles a singular Σ_ε.

    Args:
        key: PRNG key consumed by this call.
        obs: Observation vector y.
        obs_noise: Observation-error covariance Σ_ε.
        n_ensemble: Number of perturbed copies N_ℰ.

    Returns:
        The perturbed observations y⁽ᵉ⁾, one row per member.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``n_ensemble`` is below 1, or ``obs`` does not match Σ_ε.

    Examples:
        Four copies of two observations:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import jax.random as jr
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import filterax
        >>> obs = jnp.array([1.0, 2.0])
        >>> obs_noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.1 * jnp.ones(2))
        >>> perturbed = filterax.perturbed_observations(jr.key(0), obs, obs_noise, 4)
        >>> perturbed.shape
        (4, 2)

        Zero noise returns the observations themselves:

        >>> quiet = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.zeros(2))
        >>> copies = filterax.perturbed_observations(jr.key(0), obs, quiet, 2)
        >>> copies.tolist()
        [[1.0, 2.0], [1.0, 2.0]]

        At least one copy is needed:

        >>> filterax.perturbed_observations(jr.key(0), obs, obs_noise, 0)
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        ValueError: num_samples must be at least 1, got 0.

    References:
        Burgers, van Leeuwen & Evensen (1998), *Mon. Wea. Rev.* 126, 1719–1724.
    """
    # y⁽ᵉ⁾ = y + L z⁽ᵉ⁾,   L Lᵀ = Σ_ε
    return gaussx.sample_mvn(obs, obs_noise, key=key, num_samples=n_ensemble)

docs.title: Ensemble Kalman Processes
docs.text: Iterative ensemble methods for derivative-free parameter estimation. All methods share the same outer loop — the caller supplies forward-model evaluations G(θ⁽ʲ⁾) each step, the process supplies the ensemble update rule. The Layer-2 wrappers (filterax.EKI, filterax.EKS, filterax.TEKI, filterax.UKI) handle the loop for you; the artificial-time step Δtₙ is controlled by a scheduler, and the iteration states (ProcessState, UKIState, ProcessConfig) are documented with the Protocols & Types.

docs.title: Picking a process
docs.text: Method Output UQ Forward evals / step Use when filterax.EKI Collapsing point estimate None J Default calibration; underdetermined OK (J ≥ p + 1) filterax.EKS Posterior samples Full ensemble J Posterior uncertainty matters; longer runs; pass prior_mean / prior_cov for a Bayesian prior filterax.TEKI MAP None (spread is a convergence diagnostic) J Point estimate under a Gaussian prior, without gradients filterax.UKI Parametric (μ, Σ) Calibrated Σ 2 Nₚ + 1 (fixed) Moderate Nₚ ≲ 100, deterministic, reproducible filterax.processes.ETKI Gaussian posterior, for linear G Via spread J The ETKF square-root transform at Γ / Δt. Over a schedule with Σ Δt = 1 it reaches the Gaussian posterior for a linear G, keeping spread where EKI collapses it filterax.processes.GNKI MAP + ensemble spread Via spread J Well-conditioned, fast convergence, requires J > Nₚ filterax.processes.SparseInversion Sparse point estimate None J Variable selection, sparse parameter recovery

docs.title: What each model targets
docs.text:
For a Bayesian inverse problem with prior \(\mathcal{N}(m_0, \Sigma_0)\) and noise \(\Gamma\), the models converge to different things:

  • EKI: a least-squares fit to \(y\) within the span of the initial ensemble. The prior enters only through that ensemble.
  • TEKI: the MAP of \(\tfrac{1}{2}\|y - G(\theta)\|^2_{\Gamma^{-1}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\|\theta - m_0\|^2_{\Sigma_0^{-1}}\).
  • EKS with prior_mean / prior_cov: samples of the posterior \(p(\theta \mid y)\). Without them, samples of the likelihood (a flat prior).
  • UKI: a Gaussian approximation, with the initial \((\mu_0, \Sigma_0)\) acting as the prior. Exact for a linear \(G\).

docs.title: Decision tree
docs.text:
1. Need posterior samples? → EKS
  2. Need calibrated parametric covariance? → UKI (if Nₚ ≲ 100)
  3. Sparse parameters? → SparseInversion
  4. Ill-posed / need prior regularisation? → TEKI
  5. Well-conditioned, want fast convergence? → GNKI (if J > Nₚ)
  6. Otherwise → EKI (simple, robust default)

class EKI(eqx.Module, strict=True):
    r"""Ensemble Kalman Inversion — full ``init → update`` run loop.

    Composes a :class:`forward_fn` (the simulator) with a Layer-1
    :class:`~filterax._processes._processes.EKI` and a scheduler. Returns the
    final parameter ensemble plus per-iteration history.

    Attributes:
        forward_fn: ``θ → G(θ)`` mapping. Applied with :func:`jax.vmap`
            over the ensemble.
        obs: Observation vector ``y``.
        noise_cov: Observation noise covariance ``Γ``.
        scheduler: Step-size strategy. Defaults to
            :class:`DataMisfitController` which terminates when
            ``algo_time → 1``. Ignored when ``config`` is provided —
            see ``config`` below.
        config: Optional :class:`ProcessConfig`. When provided, **both**
            its ``scheduler`` and ``n_iterations`` fields take precedence
            over the module-level ``scheduler`` and the ``50``-iteration
            default. The ``scheduler`` attribute on the L2 module then
            acts as a fallback used only when ``config`` is ``None``.
    """

    forward_fn: ForwardFn
    obs: Float[Array, " N_d"]
    noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator
    scheduler: AbstractScheduler = eqx.field(default_factory=DataMisfitController)
    config: ProcessConfig | None = None

    def run(self, init_particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"]) -> ProcessResult:
        sched = _resolve_scheduler(self.scheduler, self.config)
        n_iter = _resolve_n_iterations(self.config, default=50)
        return _run_ensemble(
            _EKI(scheduler=sched),
            self.forward_fn,
            init_particles,
            self.obs,
            self.noise_cov,
            n_iterations=n_iter,
            stop_at_algo_time_one=True,
        )

class EKS(eqx.Module, strict=True):
    r"""Ensemble Kalman Sampler — full run loop.

    Like :class:`EKI` but produces approximate posterior samples (the
    ensemble does *not* collapse). Uses
    :class:`~filterax._processes._processes.EKS_Process` with
    :class:`EKSStableScheduler` by default; runs the full
    ``n_iterations`` (no algo-time termination — burn-in + sampling).

    Attributes:
        forward_fn: ``θ → G(θ)``.
        obs: Observation vector ``y``.
        noise_cov: Observation noise covariance ``Γ``.
        scheduler: Step-size strategy. Use :class:`EKSStableScheduler`.
            Ignored when ``config`` is provided.
        seed: PRNG seed for the Brownian draws.
        config: Optional :class:`ProcessConfig`. When provided, **both**
            its ``scheduler`` and ``n_iterations`` fields take precedence
            over the module-level ``scheduler`` and the ``500``-iteration
            default.
        prior_mean: Prior mean ``m₀``. With ``prior_cov``, the ensemble
            samples the posterior ``p(θ | y) ∝ p(y | θ) 𝒩(θ; m₀, Σ₀)``;
            without them, the likelihood alone (a flat prior).
        prior_cov: Prior covariance ``Σ₀``.
    """

    forward_fn: ForwardFn
    obs: Float[Array, " N_d"]
    noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator
    scheduler: AbstractScheduler = eqx.field(default_factory=EKSStableScheduler)
    seed: int = eqx.field(static=True, default=0)
    config: ProcessConfig | None = None
    prior_mean: Float[Array, " N_p"] | None = None
    prior_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator | None = None

    def run(self, init_particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"]) -> ProcessResult:
        sched = _resolve_scheduler(self.scheduler, self.config)
        n_iter = _resolve_n_iterations(self.config, default=500)
        return _run_ensemble(
            _EKS(
                scheduler=sched,
                key=self.seed,
                prior_mean=self.prior_mean,
                prior_cov=self.prior_cov,
            ),
            self.forward_fn,
            init_particles,
            self.obs,
            self.noise_cov,
            n_iterations=n_iter,
            stop_at_algo_time_one=False,
        )

docs.title: TEKI
docs.text:
Bases: Module

Tikhonov Ensemble Kalman Inversion — full run loop to the MAP.

EKI on the augmented system \(\tilde G(\theta) = (G(\theta), \theta)\), \(\tilde y = (y, m_0)\), \(\tilde\Gamma = \mathrm{blockdiag}(\Gamma, \Sigma_0)\) (Chada, Stuart & Tong 2020). The prior enters as data, so the iteration targets the maximum a posteriori estimate

\[ \theta^* = \arg\min_\theta\; \tfrac{1}{2} \|y - G(\theta)\|^2_{\Gamma^{-1}} + \tfrac{1}{2} \|\theta - m_0\|^2_{\Sigma_0^{-1}}, \]

whereas :class:EKI converges toward a least-squares fit in the span of the initial ensemble. The MAP is a fixed point of every step, so the run does not stop at algo_time = 1; it runs n_iterations steps while the deterministic ensemble contracts onto it. The final ensemble spread is a convergence diagnostic, not a posterior uncertainty; use :class:EKS with the same prior for samples.

Attributes:

Name Type Description forward_fn ForwardFn

θ → G(θ).

obs Float[Array, ' N_d']

Observation vector y.

noise_cov AbstractLinearOperator

Observation noise covariance Γ.

prior_mean Float[Array, ' N_p']

Prior mean m₀.

prior_cov AbstractLinearOperator

Prior covariance Σ₀.

scheduler AbstractScheduler

Step-size strategy (default FixedScheduler(dt=1.0), one augmented Kalman update per iteration). Ignored when config is provided.

config ProcessConfig | None

Optional :class:ProcessConfig. When provided, both its scheduler and n_iterations fields take precedence over the module-level scheduler and the 200-iteration default.

Examples:

>>> import jax, jax.numpy as jnp, lineax as lx
>>> import filterax as flx
>>> F = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.5], [-0.3, 1.2], [0.7, 0.1]])
>>> y = jnp.array([0.9, -1.4, 0.6])
>>> teki = flx.TEKI(
...     forward_fn=lambda th: F @ th,
...     obs=y,
...     noise_cov=lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.1 * jnp.ones(3)),
...     prior_mean=jnp.zeros(2),
...     prior_cov=lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(2)),
... )
>>> init = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(0), (50, 2))
>>> teki.run(init).mean.shape
(2,)

class TEKI(eqx.Module, strict=True):
    r"""Tikhonov Ensemble Kalman Inversion — full run loop to the MAP.

    EKI on the augmented system $\tilde G(\theta) = (G(\theta), \theta)$,
    $\tilde y = (y, m_0)$, $\tilde\Gamma = \mathrm{blockdiag}(\Gamma, \Sigma_0)$
    (Chada, Stuart & Tong 2020). The prior enters as data, so the
    iteration targets the maximum a posteriori estimate

    $$
    \theta^* = \arg\min_\theta\;
        \tfrac{1}{2} \|y - G(\theta)\|^2_{\Gamma^{-1}}
        + \tfrac{1}{2} \|\theta - m_0\|^2_{\Sigma_0^{-1}},
    $$

    whereas :class:`EKI` converges toward a least-squares fit in the span
    of the initial ensemble. The MAP is a fixed point of every step, so
    the run does not stop at ``algo_time = 1``; it runs ``n_iterations``
    steps while the deterministic ensemble contracts onto it. The final
    ensemble spread is a convergence diagnostic, not a posterior
    uncertainty; use :class:`EKS` with the same prior for samples.

    Attributes:
        forward_fn: ``θ → G(θ)``.
        obs: Observation vector ``y``.
        noise_cov: Observation noise covariance ``Γ``.
        prior_mean: Prior mean ``m₀``.
        prior_cov: Prior covariance ``Σ₀``.
        scheduler: Step-size strategy (default ``FixedScheduler(dt=1.0)``,
            one augmented Kalman update per iteration). Ignored when
            ``config`` is provided.
        config: Optional :class:`ProcessConfig`. When provided, **both**
            its ``scheduler`` and ``n_iterations`` fields take precedence
            over the module-level ``scheduler`` and the ``200``-iteration
            default.

    Examples:
        >>> import jax, jax.numpy as jnp, lineax as lx
        >>> import filterax as flx
        >>> F = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.5], [-0.3, 1.2], [0.7, 0.1]])
        >>> y = jnp.array([0.9, -1.4, 0.6])
        >>> teki = flx.TEKI(
        ...     forward_fn=lambda th: F @ th,
        ...     obs=y,
        ...     noise_cov=lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.1 * jnp.ones(3)),
        ...     prior_mean=jnp.zeros(2),
        ...     prior_cov=lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.ones(2)),
        ... )
        >>> init = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(0), (50, 2))
        >>> teki.run(init).mean.shape
        (2,)
    """

    forward_fn: ForwardFn
    obs: Float[Array, " N_d"]
    noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator
    prior_mean: Float[Array, " N_p"]
    prior_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator
    scheduler: AbstractScheduler = eqx.field(
        default_factory=lambda: FixedScheduler(dt=1.0)
    )
    config: ProcessConfig | None = None

    def run(self, init_particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"]) -> ProcessResult:
        sched = _resolve_scheduler(self.scheduler, self.config)
        n_iter = _resolve_n_iterations(self.config, default=200)
        return _run_ensemble(
            _TEKI(
                scheduler=sched, prior_mean=self.prior_mean, prior_cov=self.prior_cov
            ),
            self.forward_fn,
            init_particles,
            self.obs,
            self.noise_cov,
            n_iterations=n_iter,
            stop_at_algo_time_one=False,
        )

Maintains μₙ and Σₙ rather than a random ensemble; uses 2 Nₚ + 1 deterministic sigma points per step.

Observation noise covariance Γ.

class UKI(eqx.Module, strict=True):
    r"""Unscented Kalman Inversion — full parametric run loop.

    Maintains ``μₙ`` and ``Σₙ`` rather than a random ensemble; uses
    ``2 Nₚ + 1`` deterministic sigma points per step.

    Attributes:
        forward_fn: ``θ → G(θ)``.
        obs: Observation vector ``y``.
        noise_cov: Observation noise covariance ``Γ``.
        scheduler: Step-size strategy. Ignored when ``config`` is
            provided.
        alpha, beta, kappa: Unscented tuning parameters; see
            :func:`~filterax._processes._processes.sigma_points`.
        config: Optional :class:`ProcessConfig`. When provided, **both**
            its ``scheduler`` and ``n_iterations`` fields take precedence
            over the module-level ``scheduler`` and the ``50``-iteration
            default.
    """

    forward_fn: ForwardFn
    obs: Float[Array, " N_d"]
    noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator
    scheduler: AbstractScheduler = eqx.field(default_factory=DataMisfitController)
    alpha: float = eqx.field(static=True, default=1.0)
    beta: float = eqx.field(static=True, default=2.0)
    kappa: float = eqx.field(static=True, default=0.0)
    config: ProcessConfig | None = None

    def run(
        self,
        init_mean: Float[Array, " N_p"],
        init_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> ProcessResult:
        sched = _resolve_scheduler(self.scheduler, self.config)
        n_iter = _resolve_n_iterations(self.config, default=50)
        process = _UKI(
            scheduler=sched,
            alpha=self.alpha,
            beta=self.beta,
            kappa=self.kappa,
        )
        state = process.init_parametric(init_mean, init_cov, self.obs, self.noise_cov)
        # Drive the loop in parametric form for clarity; sample-point
        # evaluation happens once per iteration.
        from filterax._processes._processes import sigma_points

        algo_time = jnp.asarray(0.0)
        algo_times: list[Float[Array, ""]] = []
        converged = False
        actual = 0
        for _ in range(n_iter):
            points, _wm, _wc = sigma_points(
                state.mean,
                state.covariance,
                alpha=self.alpha,
                beta=self.beta,
                kappa=self.kappa,
            )
            evals = _vmap_forward(self.forward_fn, points)
            # Determine dt via the scheduler — wrap the parametric state
            # in a ProcessState shim so DataMisfitController can see the
            # forward evals.
            shim = ProcessState(
                particles=points,
                forward_evals=evals,
                obs=self.obs,
                noise_cov=self.noise_cov,
                step=state.step,
                algo_time=algo_time,
            )
            dt = sched.get_dt(shim)
            state = process.update_parametric(
                state, evals, obs=self.obs, noise_cov=self.noise_cov, dt=dt
            )
            algo_time = algo_time + dt
            algo_times.append(algo_time)
            actual += 1
            if float(algo_time) >= 1.0 - 1e-9:
                converged = True
                break

        return ProcessResult(
            particles=None,
            mean=state.mean,
            covariance=state.covariance,
            history_particles=None,
            history_algo_time=jnp.stack(algo_times) if algo_times else jnp.zeros(0),
            n_iterations=actual,
            converged=converged,
        )

docs.text:
Bases: AbstractProcess

Ensemble Kalman Inversion (Iglesias, Law & Stuart 2013).

Iterative ensemble method that drives θ⁽ʲ⁾ toward a MAP / regularised-least-squares solution. The update for each member:

\[ \theta^{(j)}_{n+1} = \theta^{(j)}_n + C^{\theta G}_n \big(C^{G G}_n + \Delta t_n^{-1} \Gamma\big)^{-1} \big(y - G(\theta^{(j)}_n)\big) \]

The ensemble collapses to a point as algo_time → 1: spread → 0, no posterior uncertainty (see :class:EKS_Process if you need samples). Works in the underdetermined regime J < Nₚ.

Attributes:

Name Type Description scheduler AbstractScheduler

Step-size strategy. Use :class:~filterax.DataMisfitController for the standard adaptive recipe.

Examples:

>>> import jax
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> from filterax import FixedScheduler
>>> from filterax.processes import EKI
>>> G = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.5], [-0.3, 1.2]])
>>> obs = jnp.array([0.5, 0.9])
>>> noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.1 * jnp.ones(2))
>>> eki = EKI(scheduler=FixedScheduler(dt=1.0))
>>> particles = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(0), (4, 2))
>>> state = eki.init(particles, obs, noise)
>>> evals = jax.vmap(lambda theta: G @ theta)(state.particles)
>>> state = eki.update(state, evals)
>>> state.particles.shape, int(state.step)
((4, 2), 1)
Source code in src/filterax/_processes/_processes.py 
class EKI(AbstractProcess, strict=True):
    r"""Ensemble Kalman Inversion (Iglesias, Law & Stuart 2013).

    Iterative ensemble method that drives ``θ⁽ʲ⁾`` toward a MAP /
    regularised-least-squares solution. The update for each member:

    $$
    \theta^{(j)}_{n+1} = \theta^{(j)}_n + C^{\theta G}_n
        \big(C^{G G}_n + \Delta t_n^{-1} \Gamma\big)^{-1}
        \big(y - G(\theta^{(j)}_n)\big)
    $$

    The ensemble collapses to a point as ``algo_time → 1``: spread → 0,
    no posterior uncertainty (see :class:`EKS_Process` if you need
    samples). Works in the underdetermined regime ``J < Nₚ``.

    Attributes:
        scheduler: Step-size strategy. Use
            :class:`~filterax.DataMisfitController` for the standard
            adaptive recipe.

    Examples:
        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> from filterax import FixedScheduler
        >>> from filterax.processes import EKI
        >>> G = jnp.array([[1.0, 0.5], [-0.3, 1.2]])
        >>> obs = jnp.array([0.5, 0.9])
        >>> noise = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(0.1 * jnp.ones(2))
        >>> eki = EKI(scheduler=FixedScheduler(dt=1.0))
        >>> particles = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(0), (4, 2))
        >>> state = eki.init(particles, obs, noise)
        >>> evals = jax.vmap(lambda theta: G @ theta)(state.particles)
        >>> state = eki.update(state, evals)
        >>> state.particles.shape, int(state.step)
        ((4, 2), 1)
    """

    scheduler: AbstractScheduler

    def init(
        self,
        particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"],
        obs: Float[Array, " N_d"],
        noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        check_ensemble_size(particles.shape[0])
        N_d = obs.shape[0]
        # Forward evaluations are filled in on the first update(); seed
        # with zeros so the state shape is JIT-stable.
        zero_evals = jnp.zeros((particles.shape[0], N_d), dtype=particles.dtype)
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles,
            forward_evals=zero_evals,
            obs=obs,
            noise_cov=noise_cov,
            step=jnp.asarray(0, dtype=jnp.int32),
            algo_time=jnp.asarray(0.0, dtype=particles.dtype),
        )

    def update(
        self,
        state: ProcessState,
        forward_evals: Float[Array, "J N_d"],
        **_: Any,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        # Drop the fresh evals into state so the scheduler's misfit
        # computation sees them.
        state_now = _with_evals(state, forward_evals)
        dt = self.scheduler.get_dt(state_now)
        particles_new = _eki_update(
            state.particles, forward_evals, state.obs, state.noise_cov, dt
        )
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles_new,
            forward_evals=forward_evals,
            obs=state.obs,
            noise_cov=state.noise_cov,
            step=state.step + 1,
            algo_time=state.algo_time + dt,
        )

docs.title: EKS_Process
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractProcess

Ensemble Kalman Sampler / ALDI (Garbuno-Inigo et al. 2020).

Interacting-Langevin ensemble that does not collapse — at stationarity the particles are approximate samples from the posterior p(θ | y). The per-step update is the EKI drift plus a finite-sample mean correction and an ensemble-preconditioned Brownian noise:

\[ \mathrm{d}\theta^{(j)} = C^{\theta G} \Gamma^{-1} \big(y - G^{(j)}\big)\, \mathrm{d}t - C^{\theta\theta} \Sigma_0^{-1} \big(\theta^{(j)} - m_0\big)\, \mathrm{d}t - (N_p + 1)\, J^{-1} \big(\theta^{(j)} - \bar{\theta}\big)\, \mathrm{d}t + \sqrt{2\, C^{\theta\theta}}\; \mathrm{d}W^{(j)} \]

The prior term is present only when prior_mean and prior_cov are given; without them the stationary law is the likelihood alone (a flat prior), which is the behaviour before the prior was added. The prior term is taken implicitly in θ, as in Garbuno-Inigo et al. (2020, §4), so a prior much tighter than the ensemble contracts the particles toward m₀ for any Δt instead of amplifying them.

The discrete-time recipe used here matches Garbuno-Inigo §4: an EKI-style mean update (with Δt⁻¹ Γ tempering), the (Nₚ + 1)/J drift term, and a noise term scaled by the ensemble-space sqrt of Cᶿᶿ (which avoids the dense Nₚ × Nₚ Cholesky — see comments below).

Use :class:~filterax.EKSStableScheduler to keep Δt small against the posterior's stiffness, which sets the sampling bias.

Attributes:

Name Type Description scheduler AbstractScheduler

Step-size controller. Prefer EKSStableScheduler.

key PRNGKeyArray

Base PRNG key for the Brownian draws. Each step uses jr.fold_in(key, state.step) so successive updates are independent without manual key splitting.

prior_mean Float[Array, ' N_p'] | None

Prior mean m₀ ∈ ℝ^{Nₚ}, or None for a flat prior. Give it together with prior_cov.

prior_cov AbstractLinearOperator | None

Prior covariance Σ₀, or None for a flat prior. Σ₀⁻¹ is applied through :func:gaussx.solve_rows, never formed densely.

Source code in src/filterax/_processes/_processes.py 
class EKS_Process(AbstractProcess, strict=True):
    r"""Ensemble Kalman Sampler / ALDI (Garbuno-Inigo et al. 2020).

    Interacting-Langevin ensemble that does **not** collapse — at
    stationarity the particles are approximate samples from the
    posterior ``p(θ | y)``. The per-step update is the EKI drift plus a
    finite-sample mean correction and an ensemble-preconditioned
    Brownian noise:

    $$
    \mathrm{d}\theta^{(j)} =
        C^{\theta G} \Gamma^{-1} \big(y - G^{(j)}\big)\, \mathrm{d}t
        - C^{\theta\theta} \Sigma_0^{-1} \big(\theta^{(j)} - m_0\big)\,
          \mathrm{d}t
        - (N_p + 1)\, J^{-1} \big(\theta^{(j)} - \bar{\theta}\big)\,
          \mathrm{d}t
        + \sqrt{2\, C^{\theta\theta}}\; \mathrm{d}W^{(j)}
    $$

    The prior term is present only when ``prior_mean`` and ``prior_cov``
    are given; without them the stationary law is the likelihood alone
    (a flat prior), which is the behaviour before the prior was added.
    The prior term is taken implicitly in θ, as in Garbuno-Inigo et al.
    (2020, §4), so a prior much tighter than the ensemble contracts the
    particles toward ``m₀`` for any ``Δt`` instead of amplifying them.

    The discrete-time recipe used here matches Garbuno-Inigo §4: an
    EKI-style mean update (with ``Δt⁻¹ Γ`` tempering), the
    ``(Nₚ + 1)/J`` drift term, and a noise term scaled by the
    *ensemble-space* sqrt of ``Cᶿᶿ`` (which avoids the dense ``Nₚ × Nₚ``
    Cholesky — see comments below).

    Use :class:`~filterax.EKSStableScheduler` to keep ``Δt`` small against
    the posterior's stiffness, which sets the sampling bias.

    Attributes:
        scheduler: Step-size controller. Prefer EKSStableScheduler.
        key: Base PRNG key for the Brownian draws. Each step uses
            ``jr.fold_in(key, state.step)`` so successive updates are
            independent without manual key splitting.
        prior_mean: Prior mean ``m₀ ∈ ℝ^{Nₚ}``, or ``None`` for a flat
            prior. Give it together with ``prior_cov``.
        prior_cov: Prior covariance ``Σ₀``, or ``None`` for a flat prior.
            ``Σ₀⁻¹`` is applied through :func:`gaussx.solve_rows`, never
            formed densely.
    """

    scheduler: AbstractScheduler
    key: PRNGKeyArray
    prior_mean: Float[Array, " N_p"] | None
    prior_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator | None

    def __init__(
        self,
        scheduler: AbstractScheduler,
        key: PRNGKeyArray | int = 0,
        prior_mean: Float[Array, " N_p"] | None = None,
        prior_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator | None = None,
    ):
        if (prior_mean is None) != (prior_cov is None):
            raise ValueError(
                "EKS_Process needs both prior_mean and prior_cov, or neither."
            )
        self.scheduler = scheduler
        self.key = jr.PRNGKey(key) if isinstance(key, int) else key
        self.prior_mean = prior_mean
        self.prior_cov = prior_cov

    def init(
        self,
        particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"],
        obs: Float[Array, " N_d"],
        noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        check_ensemble_size(particles.shape[0])
        N_d = obs.shape[0]
        zero_evals = jnp.zeros((particles.shape[0], N_d), dtype=particles.dtype)
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles,
            forward_evals=zero_evals,
            obs=obs,
            noise_cov=noise_cov,
            step=jnp.asarray(0, dtype=jnp.int32),
            algo_time=jnp.asarray(0.0, dtype=particles.dtype),
            prior_cov=self.prior_cov,
        )

    def update(
        self,
        state: ProcessState,
        forward_evals: Float[Array, "J N_d"],
        **_: Any,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        state_now = _with_evals(state, forward_evals)
        dt = self.scheduler.get_dt(state_now)
        J, N_p = state.particles.shape

        # 1. EKI-style drift toward the data.
        particles_drifted = _eki_update(
            state.particles, forward_evals, state.obs, state.noise_cov, dt
        )

        # 2. Mean-pull term ``− (Nₚ + 1) / J (θ − θ̄) Δt``.
        anom = ensemble_anomalies(state.particles)
        drift_pull = -((N_p + 1) / J) * dt * anom

        # 3. Ensemble-preconditioned noise:
        #     η⁽ʲ⁾ = √(2 Δt) · sqrt(Cᶿᶿ) · ξ⁽ʲ⁾,    ξ ~ 𝒩(0, I_{Nₚ}).
        # Using the ensemble sqrt ``sqrt(Cᶿᶿ) = X′ᵀ / √(J − 1)`` (i.e.
        # the LowRankUpdate's ``U`` factor) lets us draw the noise in
        # ensemble space (J-dimensional) and lift it: cost ``O(J²·Nₚ)``
        # instead of a ``Nₚ × Nₚ`` dense Cholesky.
        step_key = jr.fold_in(self.key, state.step)
        xi = jr.normal(step_key, (J, J), dtype=state.particles.dtype)
        # The ensemble sqrt has shape (Nₚ, J): U = X′ᵀ / √(J−1).
        # So η = √(2 Δt) · ξ U ᵀ, applied row-wise: η⁽ʲ⁾ = √(2 Δt) Σₖ ξⱼₖ Uᵀₖ
        # which collapses to ``ξ @ X′ / √(J−1)``.
        noise = (
            jnp.sqrt(2.0 * dt) * einx.dot("j k, k p -> j p", xi, anom) / jnp.sqrt(J - 1)
        )

        particles_new = particles_drifted + drift_pull + noise

        # 4. Prior drift ``− Δt Cᶿᶿ Σ₀⁻¹ (θ⁽ʲ⁾ − m₀)``, taken implicitly in
        #    θ (Garbuno-Inigo et al. 2020, §4) so a prior tighter than the
        #    ensemble cannot destabilise the step:
        #        θ ← θ* − (I + Δt C Σ₀⁻¹)⁻¹ Δt C Σ₀⁻¹ (θ* − m₀),
        #    θ* being the explicit update above. With C = U Uᵀ,
        #    U = X′ᵀ / √(J − 1), the push-through identity gives
        #        (I + Δt U Uᵀ Σ₀⁻¹)⁻¹ Δt U Uᵀ Σ₀⁻¹
        #            = Δt U (I_J + Δt Uᵀ Σ₀⁻¹ U)⁻¹ Uᵀ Σ₀⁻¹,
        #    so only a J × J system is solved and no Nₚ × Nₚ matrix is formed.
        if self.prior_mean is not None and self.prior_cov is not None:
            offset = einx.subtract(
                "j p, p -> j p", particles_new, self.prior_mean
            )  # (J, Nₚ)
            precision_offset = gaussx.solve_rows(self.prior_cov, offset)  # (J, Nₚ)
            precision_anom = gaussx.solve_rows(self.prior_cov, anom)  # (J, Nₚ)
            # Uᵀ Σ₀⁻¹ U = X′ Σ₀⁻¹ X′ᵀ / (J − 1)
            gram = einx.dot("k p, l p -> k l", anom, precision_anom) / (J - 1)
            system = jnp.eye(J, dtype=gram.dtype) + dt * gram  # (J, J)
            # Uᵀ Σ₀⁻¹ (θ*ⱼ − m₀), one column per member
            rhs = einx.dot("k p, j p -> k j", anom, precision_offset) / jnp.sqrt(J - 1)
            coeff = jnp.linalg.solve(system, rhs)  # (J, J)
            correction = dt * einx.dot("k j, k p -> j p", coeff, anom) / jnp.sqrt(J - 1)
            particles_new = particles_new - correction
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles_new,
            forward_evals=forward_evals,
            obs=state.obs,
            noise_cov=state.noise_cov,
            step=state.step + 1,
            algo_time=state.algo_time + dt,
            prior_cov=state.prior_cov,
        )

docs.text:
Bases: AbstractProcess

Unscented Kalman Inversion (Huang, Schneider & Stuart 2022).

Parametric inversion that maintains a Gaussian belief θ ~ 𝒩(μₙ, Σₙ) instead of an explicit ensemble. Each step generates 2 Nₚ + 1 sigma points, evaluates the forward model on them, and applies a Kalman update on the unscented statistics:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mu_{n+1} &= \mu_n + C^{\theta y} S_n^{-1} \big(y - \bar{y}\big) \\ \Sigma_{n+1} &= \Sigma_n - C^{\theta y} S_n^{-1} C^{\theta y \top}, \qquad S_n = C^{yy} + \Delta t^{-1} \Gamma \end{aligned} \]

where ȳ = Σₖ Wᵐₖ ŷₖ is the weighted mean of the evaluations.

Deterministic (no sampling noise), no ensemble collapse, and the covariance Σₙ gives a calibrated posterior in the linear-Gaussian case.

The L1 protocol uses :class:ProcessState for compatibility with DataMisfitController — the field particles carries the sigma points (last 2 Nₚ + 1 evaluations); the parametric state lives in :class:UKIState and is returned by :meth:init_parametric / :meth:update_parametric for callers that prefer the explicit form.

Attributes:

Name Type Description scheduler AbstractScheduler

Step-size strategy.

alpha float

Unscented spread parameter; usually small (e.g. 1e-3) for highly nonlinear G, 1.0 for benign problems.

beta float

Prior moment weighting; 2.0 is optimal for Gaussian priors.

kappa float

Secondary scaling, usually 0 or 3 − Nₚ.

Source code in src/filterax/_processes/_processes.py 
class UKI(AbstractProcess, strict=True):
    r"""Unscented Kalman Inversion (Huang, Schneider & Stuart 2022).

    Parametric inversion that maintains a Gaussian belief
    ``θ ~ 𝒩(μₙ, Σₙ)`` instead of an explicit ensemble. Each step
    generates ``2 Nₚ + 1`` sigma points, evaluates the forward model on
    them, and applies a Kalman update on the unscented statistics:

    $$
    \begin{aligned}
    \mu_{n+1} &= \mu_n
        + C^{\theta y} S_n^{-1} \big(y - \bar{y}\big) \\
    \Sigma_{n+1} &= \Sigma_n
        - C^{\theta y} S_n^{-1} C^{\theta y \top},
        \qquad S_n = C^{yy} + \Delta t^{-1} \Gamma
    \end{aligned}
    $$

    where ``ȳ = Σₖ Wᵐₖ ŷₖ`` is the weighted mean of the evaluations.

    Deterministic (no sampling noise), no ensemble collapse, and the
    covariance ``Σₙ`` gives a calibrated posterior in the linear-Gaussian
    case.

    The L1 protocol uses :class:`ProcessState` for compatibility with
    ``DataMisfitController`` — the field ``particles`` carries the sigma
    points (last 2 Nₚ + 1 evaluations); the parametric state lives in
    :class:`UKIState` and is returned by :meth:`init_parametric` /
    :meth:`update_parametric` for callers that prefer the explicit form.

    Attributes:
        scheduler: Step-size strategy.
        alpha: Unscented spread parameter; usually small (e.g. ``1e-3``)
            for highly nonlinear ``G``, ``1.0`` for benign problems.
        beta: Prior moment weighting; ``2.0`` is optimal for Gaussian
            priors.
        kappa: Secondary scaling, usually ``0`` or ``3 − Nₚ``.
    """

    scheduler: AbstractScheduler
    alpha: float = eqx.field(static=True, default=1.0)
    beta: float = eqx.field(static=True, default=2.0)
    kappa: float = eqx.field(static=True, default=0.0)

    # --- parametric API ---------------------------------------------------

    def init_parametric(
        self,
        mean: Float[Array, " N_p"],
        covariance: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
        obs: Float[Array, " N_d"],
        noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> UKIState:
        """Initialise the parametric ``(μ, Σ)`` state."""
        return UKIState(
            mean=mean,
            covariance=covariance,
            step=jnp.asarray(0, dtype=jnp.int32),
        )

    def update_parametric(
        self,
        state: UKIState,
        forward_evals: Float[Array, "twoNp1 N_d"],
        *,
        obs: Float[Array, " N_d"],
        noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
        dt: Float[Array, ""],
    ) -> UKIState:
        r"""One UKI step on the parametric state.

        Args:
            state: Current ``(μₙ, Σₙ)`` belief.
            forward_evals: Forward-model evaluations at the
                ``2 Nₚ + 1`` sigma points (in the order returned by
                :func:`sigma_points`).
            obs: Observation vector.
            noise_cov: Observation noise covariance ``Γ``.
            dt: Step size for this iteration.

        Returns:
            Updated :class:`UKIState`.
        """
        points, w_mean, w_cov = sigma_points(
            state.mean,
            state.covariance,
            alpha=self.alpha,
            beta=self.beta,
            kappa=self.kappa,
        )
        # Δt enters once, through Δt⁻¹ Γ in the innovation covariance. The standard
        # covariance form, since UKI's joint moments are its definition.
        mean_new, Sigma_new, _ = gaussx.sigma_point_kalman_update(
            points,
            forward_evals,
            state.mean,
            state.covariance,
            obs,
            _safe_inv_dt(dt) * noise_cov.as_matrix(),
            mean_weights=w_mean,
            cov_weights=w_cov,
            joseph=False,
        )
        return UKIState(
            mean=mean_new,
            covariance=lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
                Sigma_new, tags=lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
            ),
            step=state.step + 1,
        )

    # --- AbstractProcess (ensemble-typed) API ---------------------------------

    def init(
        self,
        particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"],
        obs: Float[Array, " N_d"],
        noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        r"""Initialise from an ensemble proxy for the parametric belief.

        Computes the empirical mean and covariance of ``particles`` and
        stores them in the leading sigma point block. Provided so UKI
        slots into the same ``init / update`` loop as the
        ensemble-typed processes; for the cleaner parametric API use
        :meth:`init_parametric` / :meth:`update_parametric`.
        """
        check_ensemble_size(particles.shape[0])
        mean = ensemble_mean(particles)
        cov_op = gaussx.ensemble_covariance(particles, bessel=True)
        cov = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(
            cov_op.as_matrix(), tags=lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
        )
        points, _wm0, _wc0 = sigma_points(
            mean, cov, alpha=self.alpha, beta=self.beta, kappa=self.kappa
        )
        N_d = obs.shape[0]
        zero_evals = jnp.zeros((points.shape[0], N_d), dtype=particles.dtype)
        return ProcessState(
            particles=points,
            forward_evals=zero_evals,
            obs=obs,
            noise_cov=noise_cov,
            step=jnp.asarray(0, dtype=jnp.int32),
            algo_time=jnp.asarray(0.0, dtype=particles.dtype),
        )

    def update(
        self,
        state: ProcessState,
        forward_evals: Float[Array, "twoNp1 N_d"],
        **_: Any,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        state_now = _with_evals(state, forward_evals)
        dt = self.scheduler.get_dt(state_now)
        # Reconstruct the parametric state from the sigma points stored
        # on ``state.particles``: the first point is the mean, and the
        # sample covariance of the remaining 2 Nₚ points recovers Σ /
        # (N_p + λ).
        points = state.particles
        N_p = (points.shape[0] - 1) // 2
        mean = points[0]
        # Recover Σ from the ``Nₚ`` positive-offset sigma points alone:
        # by construction (see :func:`sigma_points`) we have
        #   χ⁺ⱼ − μ = c · [√Σ]_{:,j},   c = √(Nₚ + λ),
        # so  Σ_k (χ⁺ⱼ − μ)(χ⁺ⱼ − μ)ᵀ = c² Σ = (Nₚ + λ) Σ.
        # Dividing by ``(Nₚ + λ)`` therefore returns Σ exactly. The
        # negative-offset block is the reflection and contributes
        # nothing new, so we skip it.
        lam = self.alpha**2 * (N_p + self.kappa) - N_p
        scale = N_p + lam
        offsets = points[1 : 1 + N_p] - mean[None, :]  # (Nₚ, Nₚ)
        Sigma_mat = einx.dot("k p, k q -> p q", offsets, offsets) / scale
        Sigma_mat = 0.5 * (Sigma_mat + Sigma_mat.T)
        cov_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(Sigma_mat, tags=lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)
        parametric = UKIState(
            mean=mean,
            covariance=cov_op,
            step=state.step,
        )
        new_parametric = self.update_parametric(
            parametric, forward_evals, obs=state.obs, noise_cov=state.noise_cov, dt=dt
        )
        new_points, _wm, _wc = sigma_points(
            new_parametric.mean,
            new_parametric.covariance,
            alpha=self.alpha,
            beta=self.beta,
            kappa=self.kappa,
        )
        return ProcessState(
            particles=new_points,
            forward_evals=forward_evals,
            obs=state.obs,
            noise_cov=state.noise_cov,
            step=state.step + 1,
            algo_time=state.algo_time + dt,
        )

docs.text:
Bases: AbstractProcess

Ensemble Transform Kalman Inversion.

The ETKF square-root transform applied to the tempered likelihood, through :func:gaussx.eki_step with deterministic=True:

\[ \bar{\theta} \leftarrow \bar{\theta} + C^{\theta G} S^{-1} (y - \bar{G}), \qquad \theta' \leftarrow W \theta', \qquad W = (J - 1)^{1/2} \big((J - 1) I + G' \Delta t \Gamma^{-1} G'^{\top}\big)^{-1/2}. \]

The mean moves as in :class:EKI, but the anomalies contract at half EKI's rate as Δt → 0. For a linear G with J > Nₚ, a schedule with Σ Δtₙ = 1 lands exactly on the Gaussian posterior of the initial ensemble's mean and covariance, where :class:EKI keeps collapsing the spread.

Attributes:

Name Type Description scheduler AbstractScheduler

Step-size strategy.

class ETKI(AbstractProcess, strict=True):
    r"""Ensemble Transform Kalman Inversion.

    The ETKF square-root transform applied to the tempered likelihood, through
    :func:`gaussx.eki_step` with ``deterministic=True``:

    $$
    \bar{\theta} \leftarrow \bar{\theta} + C^{\theta G} S^{-1} (y - \bar{G}),
    \qquad
    \theta' \leftarrow W \theta',
    \qquad
    W = (J - 1)^{1/2} \big((J - 1) I + G' \Delta t \Gamma^{-1} G'^{\top}\big)^{-1/2}.
    $$

    The mean moves as in :class:`EKI`, but the anomalies contract at half EKI's
    rate as ``Δt → 0``. For a linear ``G`` with ``J > Nₚ``, a schedule with
    ``Σ Δtₙ = 1`` lands exactly on the Gaussian posterior of the initial
    ensemble's mean and covariance, where :class:`EKI` keeps collapsing the
    spread.

    Attributes:
        scheduler: Step-size strategy.
    """

    scheduler: AbstractScheduler

    def init(
        self,
        particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"],
        obs: Float[Array, " N_d"],
        noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        check_ensemble_size(particles.shape[0])
        N_d = obs.shape[0]
        zero_evals = jnp.zeros((particles.shape[0], N_d), dtype=particles.dtype)
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles,
            forward_evals=zero_evals,
            obs=obs,
            noise_cov=noise_cov,
            step=jnp.asarray(0, dtype=jnp.int32),
            algo_time=jnp.asarray(0.0, dtype=particles.dtype),
        )

    def update(
        self,
        state: ProcessState,
        forward_evals: Float[Array, "J N_d"],
        **_: Any,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        state_now = _with_evals(state, forward_evals)
        dt = self.scheduler.get_dt(state_now)
        particles_new = gaussx.eki_step(
            state.particles,
            forward_evals,
            state.obs,
            state.noise_cov,
            dt=_floored_dt(dt),
            deterministic=True,
        )
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles_new,
            forward_evals=forward_evals,
            obs=state.obs,
            noise_cov=state.noise_cov,
            step=state.step + 1,
            algo_time=state.algo_time + dt,
        )

docs.text:
Bases: AbstractProcess

Gauss-Newton Kalman Inversion.

Estimates the Jacobian explicitly from ensemble perturbations (J̃ ≈ Cᶿᴳ (Cᶿᶿ)⁻¹) and applies a Gauss-Newton update with prior pull-back:

\[ \delta\theta^{(j)} = K \big(y - G^{(j)}\big) + \big(I - K \tilde{J}\big)\big(m_0 - \theta^{(j)}\big), \qquad K = \big(\tilde{J}^{\top} \Gamma^{-1} \tilde{J} + \Sigma_0^{-1}\big)^{-1} \tilde{J}^{\top} \Gamma^{-1}. \]

Faster convergence than :class:EKI for well-conditioned problems and requires J > Nₚ so Cᶿᶿ is invertible. In the linear-Gaussian limit GNKI recovers the exact posterior mean and covariance.

Attributes:

Name Type Description scheduler AbstractScheduler

Step-size strategy.

prior_mean Float[Array, ' N_p']

Prior mean m₀ ∈ ℝ^{Nₚ}.

prior_cov AbstractLinearOperator

Prior covariance Σ₀.

jitter float

Tikhonov regularisation added to Cᶿᶿ before inversion. Needed when J is barely larger than Nₚ.

class GNKI(AbstractProcess, strict=True):
    r"""Gauss-Newton Kalman Inversion.

    Estimates the Jacobian explicitly from ensemble perturbations
    (``J̃ ≈ Cᶿᴳ (Cᶿᶿ)⁻¹``) and applies a Gauss-Newton update with prior
    pull-back:

    $$
    \delta\theta^{(j)} = K \big(y - G^{(j)}\big)
        + \big(I - K \tilde{J}\big)\big(m_0 - \theta^{(j)}\big), \qquad
    K = \big(\tilde{J}^{\top} \Gamma^{-1} \tilde{J}
        + \Sigma_0^{-1}\big)^{-1} \tilde{J}^{\top} \Gamma^{-1}.
    $$

    Faster convergence
    than :class:`EKI` for well-conditioned problems and requires
    ``J > Nₚ`` so ``Cᶿᶿ`` is invertible. In the linear-Gaussian limit
    GNKI recovers the exact posterior mean *and* covariance.

    Attributes:
        scheduler: Step-size strategy.
        prior_mean: Prior mean ``m₀ ∈ ℝ^{Nₚ}``.
        prior_cov: Prior covariance ``Σ₀``.
        jitter: Tikhonov regularisation added to ``Cᶿᶿ`` before
            inversion. Needed when ``J`` is barely larger than ``Nₚ``.
    """

    scheduler: AbstractScheduler
    prior_mean: Float[Array, " N_p"]
    prior_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator
    jitter: float = eqx.field(static=True, default=1e-6)

    def init(
        self,
        particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"],
        obs: Float[Array, " N_d"],
        noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        J, N_p = particles.shape
        check_ensemble_size(J)
        # GNKI inverts the sample parameter covariance Cᶿᶿ ∈ ℝ^{Nₚ×Nₚ}.
        # With J ≤ Nₚ that matrix has rank ≤ J − 1 < Nₚ and is singular
        # — the jitter regulariser would dominate and silently corrupt
        # the Gauss-Newton step. Fail fast so users know to switch to
        # EKI (which works in the underdetermined regime).
        if J <= N_p:  # noqa: SIM300 — phrasing matches "J > Nₚ" requirement
            raise ValueError(
                "GNKI requires J > Nₚ so the sample parameter covariance "
                f"Cᶿᶿ is invertible; got J={J} and Nₚ={N_p}. Use "
                "filterax.EKI for the underdetermined regime."
            )
        N_d = obs.shape[0]
        zero_evals = jnp.zeros((J, N_d), dtype=particles.dtype)
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles,
            forward_evals=zero_evals,
            obs=obs,
            noise_cov=noise_cov,
            step=jnp.asarray(0, dtype=jnp.int32),
            algo_time=jnp.asarray(0.0, dtype=particles.dtype),
        )

    def update(
        self,
        state: ProcessState,
        forward_evals: Float[Array, "J N_d"],
        **_: Any,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        state_now = _with_evals(state, forward_evals)
        dt = self.scheduler.get_dt(state_now)
        N_p = state.particles.shape[1]

        # Ensemble Jacobian via cross-covariance solve.
        C_theta_theta = gaussx.ensemble_covariance(
            state.particles, bessel=True
        ).as_matrix() + self.jitter * jnp.eye(N_p)
        C_theta_G = gaussx.ensemble_cross_covariance(
            state.particles, forward_evals, bessel=True
        )  # (Nₚ, N_d)
        J_tilde = jnp.linalg.solve(C_theta_theta, C_theta_G)  # (Nₚ, N_d)

        # Gain K = (J̃ᵀ Γ⁻¹ J̃ + Σ₀⁻¹)⁻¹ J̃ᵀ Γ⁻¹.
        # solve_rows treats each row of J_tilde as an N_d vector and
        # returns (Γ⁻¹ J̃)_k row-by-row → shape (Nₚ, N_d).
        Gamma_inv_J = gaussx.solve_rows(state.noise_cov, J_tilde)  # (Nₚ, N_d)
        # Σ₀⁻¹, each row solved through the prior's own structure
        prior_precision = gaussx.solve_rows(
            self.prior_cov, jnp.eye(N_p, dtype=J_tilde.dtype)
        )
        precision = einx.dot("p d, q d -> p q", J_tilde, Gamma_inv_J) + prior_precision
        precision = 0.5 * (precision + precision.T)
        K_gain = jnp.linalg.solve(precision, Gamma_inv_J)  # (Nₚ, N_d)

        # Per-member update.
        residuals = einx.subtract("d, j d -> j d", state.obs, forward_evals)
        prior_pull = einx.subtract("p, j p -> j p", self.prior_mean, state.particles)
        data_step = einx.dot("p d, j d -> j p", K_gain, residuals)
        # (I − K J̃) m₀-pull term, expanded as m₀-pull − K J̃ (m₀-pull).
        J_pull = einx.dot("p d, j p -> j d", J_tilde, prior_pull)
        prior_step = prior_pull - einx.dot("p d, j d -> j p", K_gain, J_pull)
        delta = dt * (data_step + prior_step)
        particles_new = state.particles + delta
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles_new,
            forward_evals=forward_evals,
            obs=state.obs,
            noise_cov=state.noise_cov,
            step=state.step + 1,
            algo_time=state.algo_time + dt,
        )

Sparse Ensemble Kalman Inversion (Schneider, Stuart & Wu 2022).

Standard EKI step followed by an L¹ proximal soft-threshold:

\[ \mathrm{prox}_{\lambda \|\cdot\|_1}(z)_i = \mathrm{sign}(z_i) \cdot \max\big(|z_i| - \lambda,\, 0\big) \]

drives inactive parameters exactly to zero. Useful for variable selection / sparse physics discovery / sensor placement.

Attributes:

Name Type Description scheduler AbstractScheduler

Step-size strategy.

penalty_weight float

λ > 0. Larger λ → more sparsity.

class SparseInversion(AbstractProcess, strict=True):
    r"""Sparse Ensemble Kalman Inversion (Schneider, Stuart & Wu 2022).

    Standard EKI step followed by an L¹ proximal soft-threshold:

    $$
    \mathrm{prox}_{\lambda \|\cdot\|_1}(z)_i =
        \mathrm{sign}(z_i) \cdot \max\big(|z_i| - \lambda,\, 0\big)
    $$

    drives inactive parameters exactly to zero. Useful for variable
    selection / sparse physics discovery / sensor placement.

    Attributes:
        scheduler: Step-size strategy.
        penalty_weight: ``λ > 0``. Larger ``λ`` → more sparsity.
    """

    scheduler: AbstractScheduler
    penalty_weight: float = eqx.field(static=True, default=0.1)

    def init(
        self,
        particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"],
        obs: Float[Array, " N_d"],
        noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        check_ensemble_size(particles.shape[0])
        N_d = obs.shape[0]
        zero_evals = jnp.zeros((particles.shape[0], N_d), dtype=particles.dtype)
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles,
            forward_evals=zero_evals,
            obs=obs,
            noise_cov=noise_cov,
            step=jnp.asarray(0, dtype=jnp.int32),
            algo_time=jnp.asarray(0.0, dtype=particles.dtype),
        )

    def update(
        self,
        state: ProcessState,
        forward_evals: Float[Array, "J N_d"],
        **_: Any,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        state_now = _with_evals(state, forward_evals)
        dt = self.scheduler.get_dt(state_now)
        z = _eki_update(state.particles, forward_evals, state.obs, state.noise_cov, dt)
        # Soft-threshold proximal operator scaled by Δt · λ.
        lam = self.penalty_weight * dt
        particles_new = jnp.sign(z) * jnp.maximum(jnp.abs(z) - lam, 0.0)
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles_new,
            forward_evals=forward_evals,
            obs=state.obs,
            noise_cov=state.noise_cov,
            step=state.step + 1,
            algo_time=state.algo_time + dt,
        )

docs.text:
Bases: AbstractProcess

Tikhonov-regularised Ensemble Kalman Inversion (Chada et al. 2019).

Standard EKI on an augmented system that includes the parameters in observation space:

\[ \tilde{G}(\theta) = \big(G(\theta),\, \theta\big)^{\top}, \qquad \tilde{y} = (y,\, m_0)^{\top}, \qquad \tilde{\Gamma} = \mathrm{blockdiag}(\Gamma,\, \Sigma_0) \]

The augmented identity block in Cᶿᴳ̃ pulls particles toward the prior mean m₀ and prevents the ensemble from drifting arbitrarily far from the prior — useful for ill-posed problems where vanilla EKI diverges. Converges to the MAP estimate (not MLE).

class TEKI(AbstractProcess, strict=True):
    r"""Tikhonov-regularised Ensemble Kalman Inversion (Chada et al. 2019).

    Standard EKI on an augmented system that includes the parameters in
    observation space:

    $$
    \tilde{G}(\theta) = \big(G(\theta),\, \theta\big)^{\top}, \qquad
    \tilde{y} = (y,\, m_0)^{\top}, \qquad
    \tilde{\Gamma} = \mathrm{blockdiag}(\Gamma,\, \Sigma_0)
    $$

    The augmented identity block in ``Cᶿᴳ̃`` pulls particles toward the
    prior mean ``m₀`` and prevents the ensemble from drifting arbitrarily
    far from the prior — useful for ill-posed problems where vanilla EKI
    diverges. Converges to the MAP estimate (not MLE).

    Attributes:
        scheduler: Step-size strategy.
        prior_mean: Prior mean ``m₀ ∈ ℝ^{Nₚ}``.
        prior_cov: Prior covariance ``Σ₀``.
    """

    scheduler: AbstractScheduler
    prior_mean: Float[Array, " N_p"]
    prior_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator

    def init(
        self,
        particles: Float[Array, "J N_p"],
        obs: Float[Array, " N_d"],
        noise_cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        check_ensemble_size(particles.shape[0])
        N_d = obs.shape[0]
        N_p = particles.shape[1]
        zero_evals = jnp.zeros((particles.shape[0], N_d), dtype=particles.dtype)
        # ỹ = (y, m₀) and Γ̃ = blockdiag(Γ, Σ₀), stored so each update and the
        # scheduler see the augmented system.
        _, aug_obs, aug_noise = gaussx.tikhonov_augment(
            particles, zero_evals, obs, noise_cov, self.prior_mean, self.prior_cov
        )
        zero_evals = jnp.zeros((particles.shape[0], N_d + N_p), dtype=particles.dtype)
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles,
            forward_evals=zero_evals,
            obs=aug_obs,
            noise_cov=aug_noise,
            step=jnp.asarray(0, dtype=jnp.int32),
            algo_time=jnp.asarray(0.0, dtype=particles.dtype),
        )

    def update(
        self,
        state: ProcessState,
        forward_evals: Float[Array, "J N_d"],
        **_: Any,
    ) -> ProcessState:
        # Augment evals with the particles themselves: G̃(θ⁽ʲ⁾) = (G⁽ʲ⁾, θ⁽ʲ⁾).
        aug_evals = jnp.concatenate([forward_evals, state.particles], axis=1)
        state_now = _with_evals(state, aug_evals)
        dt = self.scheduler.get_dt(state_now)
        particles_new = _eki_update(
            state.particles, aug_evals, state.obs, state.noise_cov, dt
        )
        return ProcessState(
            particles=particles_new,
            forward_evals=aug_evals,
            obs=state.obs,
            noise_cov=state.noise_cov,
            step=state.step + 1,
            algo_time=state.algo_time + dt,
        )

docs.title: sigma_points(mean: Float[Array, ' N_p'], cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator, *, alpha: float = 1.0, beta: float = 2.0, kappa: float = 0.0) -> tuple[Float[Array, 'twoNp1 N_p'], Float[Array, ' twoNp1'], Float[Array, ' twoNp1']]
docs.text:
Generate 2 Nₚ + 1 deterministic sigma points (Wan & van der Merwe 2000).

For mean μ and covariance Σ:

\[ \lambda = \alpha^2 (N_p + \kappa) - N_p, \qquad c = \sqrt{N_p + \lambda} \] \[ \chi^0 = \mu, \qquad \chi^{+}_j = \mu + c \, [\sqrt{\Sigma}]_{:,j}, \qquad \chi^{-}_j = \mu - c \, [\sqrt{\Sigma}]_{:,j} \]

with weights for the mean and covariance:

\[ \begin{aligned} W_m^0 &= \frac{\lambda}{N_p + \lambda}, & W_c^0 &= W_m^0 + (1 - \alpha^2 + \beta), \\ W_m^i &= W_c^i = \frac{1}{2 (N_p + \lambda)} & &\text{for } i \neq 0. \end{aligned} \]

Thin wrapper over :func:gaussx.sigma_points, keeping filterax's default α = 1. At that default the centre mean weight is zero, where gaussx's default α = 1e-3 recovers the moments by cancelling weights of order 1e6. √Σ is the principal root from :func:gaussx.sqrt, so a structured Σ keeps its own root and the points do not depend on the order of the parameters.

Returns:

Type Description Float[Array, 'twoNp1 N_p']

(points, mean_weights, cov_weights) with shapes

Float[Array, ' twoNp1']

(2 Nₚ + 1, Nₚ), (2 Nₚ + 1,), (2 Nₚ + 1,), in the dtype of

Float[Array, ' twoNp1']

mean.

Source code in src/filterax/_processes/_processes.py 
def sigma_points(
    mean: Float[Array, " N_p"],
    cov: lx.AbstractLinearOperator,
    *,
    alpha: float = 1.0,
    beta: float = 2.0,
    kappa: float = 0.0,
) -> tuple[
    Float[Array, "twoNp1 N_p"],
    Float[Array, " twoNp1"],
    Float[Array, " twoNp1"],
]:
    r"""Generate ``2 Nₚ + 1`` deterministic sigma points (Wan & van der Merwe 2000).

    For mean ``μ`` and covariance ``Σ``:

    $$
    \lambda = \alpha^2 (N_p + \kappa) - N_p, \qquad
    c = \sqrt{N_p + \lambda}
    $$

    $$
    \chi^0 = \mu, \qquad
    \chi^{+}_j = \mu + c \, [\sqrt{\Sigma}]_{:,j}, \qquad
    \chi^{-}_j = \mu - c \, [\sqrt{\Sigma}]_{:,j}
    $$

    with weights for the mean and covariance:

    $$
    \begin{aligned}
    W_m^0 &= \frac{\lambda}{N_p + \lambda}, &
    W_c^0 &= W_m^0 + (1 - \alpha^2 + \beta), \\
    W_m^i &= W_c^i = \frac{1}{2 (N_p + \lambda)} & &\text{for } i \neq 0.
    \end{aligned}
    $$

    Thin wrapper over :func:`gaussx.sigma_points`, keeping filterax's default
    ``α = 1``. At that default the centre mean weight is zero, where gaussx's
    default ``α = 1e-3`` recovers the moments by cancelling weights of order
    ``1e6``. ``√Σ`` is the principal root from :func:`gaussx.sqrt`, so a
    structured ``Σ`` keeps its own root and the points do not depend on the
    order of the parameters.

    Returns:
        ``(points, mean_weights, cov_weights)`` with shapes
        ``(2 Nₚ + 1, Nₚ)``, ``(2 Nₚ + 1,)``, ``(2 Nₚ + 1,)``, in the dtype of
        ``mean``.
    """
    return gaussx.sigma_points(mean, cov, alpha=alpha, beta=beta, kappa=kappa)

docs.title: Protocols & Types
docs.text: filterax components talk to each other through a small set of abstract interfaces (all equinox.Module subclasses, so implementations are immutable pytrees that survive jit / grad / vmap) and a matching set of typed containers. Implement the Abstract* classes to plug your own dynamics, observation operators, localizers, or inflators into the Layer-2 loops; the containers are what those loops accept and return.
